'''Stephen Patrick Long''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (13 August 1950 – 9 September 2025) was a British-born American environmental [[plant physiologist]]<ref name=gs>{{Google scholar id}}</ref> and member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] studying how to improve [[photosynthesis]] to increase the yield of food and biofuel crops.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.researcherid.com/ProfileView.action?returnCode=ROUTER.Success&Init=Yes&SrcApp=CR&queryString=KG0UuZjN5WlSDh3Egt%252BvR6bXf2wrasMjnRM0YvWOqH4%253D&SID=3EIWMeMaSFCkC8chn3T |title= ResearcherID |publisher= researcherid.com |accessdate=2017-06-19}}</ref> He was the Stanley O. Ikenberry Chair Professor of Plant Biology and Crop Sciences at the [[University of Illinois]] and visiting professor in Plant Sciences at [[Lancaster University]] and at Oxford University, UK.  His work, published in ''Science'',<ref>{{cite journal|title= Improving photosynthesis and crop productivity by accelerating recovery from photoprotection |journal= Science |volume= 354 |issue= 6314 |pages= 857–861 |date= 2016 |doi= 10.1126/science.aai8878 |pmid= 27856901 |last1= Kromdijk |first1= Johannes |last2= Głowacka |first2= Katarzyna |last3= Leonelli |first3= Lauriebeth |last4= Gabilly |first4= Stéphane T. |last5= Iwai |first5= Masakazu |last6= Niyogi |first6= Krishna K. |last7= Long |first7= Stephen P. |bibcode= 2016Sci...354..857K |osti= 1832459 |doi-access= free }}</ref> proved that photosynthesis can be manipulated to increase plant productivity—an idea once considered the holy grail of plant biology.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://theconversation.com/research-shows-how-to-grow-more-cassava-one-of-the-worlds-key-food-crops-68115 |title= Research shows how to grow more cassava, one of the world's key food crops |publisher= theconversation.com |date=24 January 2017 |accessdate=2017-06-19}}</ref> Long has added to our understanding of the long-term impacts of [[climate change]], such as rising levels of [[carbon dioxide]] and [[ozone]] on plants. He has briefed former president [[George W. Bush]] and the [[Holy See|Vatican]], as well as [[Bill Gates]] and [[Anne, Princess Royal]], on [[food security]] and bioenergy.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://lab.igb.illinois.edu/long/team/long/ |title= Steve Long |publisher= igb.illinois.edu  |accessdate=2017-06-21}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Long was born and raised in London, England.<ref>{{Cite Q|Q138341900}}</ref> His high school biology teacher inspired him to study plants—and famines in the 1960s encouraged him to find avenues to increase agricultural productivity.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XYXJeZdzpZE |title= Campus Insights: Steve Long |via= YouTube |date=17 March 2017 |accessdate=2017-06-19}}</ref> Long earned his bachelor's degree in agricultural botany from Reading University in 1972 and went on to earn a doctorate in plant environmental physiology from Leeds University in 1976. In 2007, [[Lancaster University]] honored Long's environmental research contributions with a doctorate of environmental science ''honoris causa''.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://lab.igb.illinois.edu/long/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/Stephen-P-Long-CV-2017_06_15.pdf |title= Stephen P. Long CV |publisher= lab.igb.illinois.edu |date=15 June 2017 |accessdate=2017-06-15}}</ref>

==Career and research==
Long joined the faculty as a lecturer at the [[University of Essex]] in 1975 and went on to become a senior lecturer (1987) and reader (1988); he obtained full professorship in 1990. In 1999, he moved to the [[University of Illinois]] and was named the Robert Emerson Professor of Plant Biology and of Crop Sciences (1999–2008). Over his career, Long has worked at [[Tate & Lyle]] Ltd. Research Centre, the [[Smithsonian Institution]] (1989), the [[University of Vienna]] (1989–1990), and [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] (1992–1999). In 2007, as the founding deputy director, Long helped launch the [[Energy Biosciences Institute]] (EBI), a 10-year, $500&nbsp;million research project that was then the largest public-private partnership between the [[University of California]] at Berkeley, [[University of Illinois]] at Urbana-Champaign, [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], and the energy company [[BP]]. In 2008, he was named the Edward William and Jane Marr Gutgsell Endowed University Professor of Crop Sciences and Plant Biology. From 2010 to 2016, he also served as a Special U.S. Government Employee (SGE) advising for the biomass programs for the [[United States Department of Energy]] and [[United States Department of Agriculture]].

In 2012, Long stepped down from leading the EBI to direct [[Realizing Increased Photosynthetic Efficiency]] (RIPE),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ripe.illinois.edu/ |title= RIPE |publisher= ripe.illinois.edu |accessdate=2017-06-21}}</ref> a $25-million-dollar research project funded by the [[Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation]] to engineer plants to photosynthesize more efficiently in order to sustainably increase worldwide food productivity. In 2017, the RIPE project received a $45 million reinvestment from the Gates Foundation, Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research (FFAR) and the UK Department for International Development.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.agri-pulse.com/articles/9864-ffar-joins-45m-project-to-boost-crop-yields-through-photosynthesis |title=FFAR joins $45M project to boost crop yields through photosynthesis |publisher=agri-pulse.com |accessdate=2018-08-09}}</ref> Long has also served as the director of two [[ARPA-E]]-funded projects: Plants Engineered to Replace Oil in Sugarcane and Sweet Sorghum (PETROSS), 2013–2018<ref>{{cite web|url=http://petross.illinois.edu/ |title=PETROSS |publisher= petross.illinois.edu |accessdate=2017-06-21}}</ref> and Transportation Energy Resource from Renewable Agriculture – Mobile Energy-Crop Phenotyping Platform (TERRA-MEPP), 2015–2019.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://terra-mepp.illinois.edu/ |title= TERRAMEPP |publisher= terra-mepp.illinois.edu |accessdate=2017-06-21}}</ref> He has also served as the deputy director of a third [[ARPA-E]]-funded project, Water Efficient Sorghum Technologies (WEST), 2016–2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://west.illinois.edu/ |title= WEST |publisher=west.illinois.edu |accessdate=2017-06-21}}</ref> In 2013, he was "selected from the faculty on the basis of their outstanding scholarship" and appointed as a Center for Advanced Studies (CAS) Professor at Illinois.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cas.illinois.edu/faculty/professors/|title=CAS Professors {{!}} CAS|website=cas.illinois.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2018-08-13}}</ref> In 2014, he joined the faculty of the [[Carl R. Woese Institute for Genomic Biology]], an interdisciplinary life sciences research institute at Illinois. In 2016, he became the Distinguished Professor in Crop Sciences FRS at [[Lancaster University]]. From 2017 to 2018, he served as the Newton Abraham visiting professor of Oxford University.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.plants.ox.ac.uk/people/professor-stephen-long|title=Newton-Abraham Visiting Professor|publisher=plants.ox.ac.uk|accessdate=2018-08-13}}</ref> In 2018, he was amongst four Illinois faculty members selected for an [[Stanley O. Ikenberry|Ikenberry]] Endowed Chair that is "deemed to be among the most distinguished honors on the campus".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.illinois.edu/view/6367/603361 |title=Faculty members selected for distinguished chairs |publisher=news.illinois.edu |accessdate=2018-08-13}}</ref> In 2019, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2019-nas-election.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430143122/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2019-nas-election.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=30 April 2019 |title=2019 NAS Election |publisher=nasonline.org |accessdate=2019-04-30}}</ref>

In addition, Long was the founding and chief editor of ''[[Global Change Biology]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title= Global Change Biology |journal = Global Change Biology|doi= 10.1111/(ISSN)1365-2486 |doi-access=free  }}</ref> He also founded ''[[GCB Bioenergy]]'',<ref>{{cite journal|title= GCB-Bioenergy |journal = GCB Bioenergy|doi= 10.1111/(ISSN)1757-1707 |doi-access= free |hdl= 11390/1101778 |hdl-access= free }}</ref> the most highly cited bioenergy journal and second most highly cited agronomy journal. In 2018, he launched a new journal ''[[in silico Plants]]'' (isP) through the Oxford University Press that will publish cross-disciplinary research at the interface between plant biology, mathematics and computer science.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.botany.one/2018/07/in-silico-plants-isp-launches-a-computational-plant-science-journal/ |title=in silico Plants (isP) launches – a computational plant science journal|date=2018-07-31 |publisher=botany.one |access-date=2018-08-13}}</ref>

He was a member of the editorial board for [[PNAS]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pnas.org/page/about/editorial-board |title = Editorial Board |website=pnas.org |access-date=2023-12-19}}</ref>

Long was the author of more than 400 scientific publications, including more than 250 peer-reviewed articles in journals such as ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''<ref>{{cite journal|title= C4 photosynthesis in plants from cool temperate regions, with particular reference to Spartina townsendii |journal= Nature |volume= 257 |issue= 5527 |pages= 622–624 |date=16 October 1975 |doi= 10.1038/257622a0 |last1= Long |first1= S. R. |last2= Long |first2= S. P. |s2cid= 206557355 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title= Feedstocks for Lignocellulosic Biofuels |journal= Science |volume= 329 |issue= 5993 |pages= 790–792 |date= 2010 |doi= 10.1126/science.1189268 |pmid= 20705851 |last1= Somerville |first1= C. |last2= Youngs |first2= H. |last3= Taylor |first3= C. |last4= Davis |first4= S. R. |bibcode= 2006Sci...312.1918L |s2cid= 2232629 }}</ref> Of particular note, he discovered the most productive land plant known<ref>{{cite journal|title= The Productivity of the C_4 Grass ''Echinochloa Polystachya'' on the Amazon Floodplain |journal= Ecology |volume= 72 |issue= 4 |pages= 1456–1463 |date=1 August 1991 |doi= 10.2307/1941118 |jstor= 1941118 |last1 = Piedade|first1 = M. T. F.|last2= Junk |first2= W. J. |last3= Long |first3= S. P. |bibcode= 1991Ecol...72.1456P }}</ref> ''[[Echinochloa polystachya]]'') and identified ''[[Miscanthus]]'' as a productive temperate plant, transforming it into a viable bioenergy crop in Europe and North America.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://lab.igb.illinois.edu/long/team/long/  |title= Steve Long |publisher= igb.illinois.edu |accessdate=2017-06-21}}</ref> He also developed the "first dynamic model of the complete photosynthetic process."<ref>{{cite web|url= http://lab.igb.illinois.edu/long/team/long/ |title= Steve Long |publisher= lab.igb.illinois.edu |accessdate=2017-06-20}}</ref> Recent work by Long has centered on how to engineer plants to photosynthesize more efficiently to increase yields of food and bioenergy crops. ==Death==
Long died on 9 September 2025, after being diagnosed with pancreatic cancer 18 months prior. He was 75.<ref name=obit>{{cite web |title=Stephen Long Obituary (1950 – 2025) - Urbana, IL - The News-Gazette |url=https://obits.mlive.com/us/obituaries/news-gazette/name/stephen-long-obituary?id=59444734 |work=News Gazette|access-date=21 September 2025 |date=13 September 2025}}</ref><ref name=raines2025>{{cite web |author1=Christine Raines |author2=Tracy Lawson |author3=Amanda Cavanagh |title=Tribute to Professor Steve Long |url=https://www.essex.ac.uk/blog/posts/2025/09/16/steve-long |publisher=University of Essex |access-date=21 September 2025 |date=16 September 2025}}</ref><ref>https://emails.illinois.edu/newsletter/48/1992217148.html</ref>

== Awards and honours ==
In 1972, Long received the University Prize from the [[University of Reading]]. From 1972 to 1975, he served as a University Scholar at the [[University of Leeds]]. He was a recipient of the Andrew Mellon Foundation personal award (1998–2003) and the McNair Movement Award (2005). He has been recognized by Clarivate Analytics (formerly Thomson Reuters) as a highly cited researcher in the field of plant and animal science every year since 2005. In 2007, the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] elected Long as a fellow. He was also chosen to be the G.E. Blackman Lecturer at the [[University of Oxford]] and the Porter Alliance Lecturer at [[Imperial College London]] in 2007. In 2008, he was named the Heilborn Lecturer at [[Northwestern University]]; the CMI Lecturer at [[Princeton University]]; the Industry Summer School Lecturer at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]; the 9th Annual Woolhouse Lecturer for the [[Society for Experimental Biology]]; and Holden Botany Lecturer at [[Sutton Bonington Campus]] in 2008. In 2009, he was named a Fellow of the [[American Society of Plant Biologists]]. In 2010, he served as the BEGC Lecturer at [[Harvard University]]. In 2012, he served as an Invited Expert on Food Security for the President's Council of Advisors on Science Technology ([[PCAST]]). In 2012, he was also honored with the Charles F. Kettering Award for Excellence in Photosynthesis Research from the [[American Society of Plant Biologists]] and the Marsh Award for Climate Change Research from the [[British Ecological Society]]. Also in 2012, he became an Elected Fellow of [[Rothamsted Research]], appointed to advise the director of the world's oldest agricultural experimental research station. In 2013, he served as the CeBiTec Annual Distinguished Lecturer at the Centrum für Biotechnologie and the 4th Annual Riley Memorial Lecturer for the [[World Food Prize]] and [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. He also received the Innovation Award from the International Society for Photosynthesis Research. In 2013, Long was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS), the oldest continually operating society that honors leading scientists and engineers. In 2016, he became an Elected Fellow of Lincoln College at the [[University of Oxford]]. Long has also been named as one of "The World’s Most Influential Scientific Minds" by Thomson Reuters.
